The Spotted catfish Arius maculatus exhibits a substantial ultimate total length, with the largest recorded individuals reaching 98.95 cm [Li = 98.95 cm]. This considerable size is typical of the genus, reflecting a life history strategy that prioritizes somatic investment before the onset of reproduction. Field surveys conducted in estuarine habitats of Southeast Asia indicate that sexual maturation, determined through macroscopic examination of gonadal development, occurs when individuals attain a total length at puberty of approximately 38 cm [Lp = approximately 38 cm]. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, derived from length-weight relationships for this species, averages around 614 grams [Wwp = around 614 grams], representing a significant proportion of the ultimate mass. This pattern of delayed maturation relative to body size is consistent with other large-bodied ariid catfishes, which typically exhibit protracted juvenile phases in productive coastal environments before transitioning to reproductive adults.

Reproductive investment in Arius maculatus has been studied primarily through captive observations and comparisons with the well-documented congener Ariopsis felis. The eggs themselves are notably large, with oocyte diameters reaching approximately 16 mm in related species, suggesting substantial maternal investment per offspring. This low fecundity but high per-offspring investment is a hallmark of K-selected life history strategies in teleosts.

This generous initial endowment is derived from the large, yolk-rich eggs characteristic of the species, which provide ample reserves to sustain the prolarva through the lecithotrophic phase until the onset of exogenous feeding. The yolk-dependent larva benefits from this substantial energy depot, which supports rapid initial growth and the development of functional feeding structures. The embryonic yolk mass, estimated from egg diameter relationships in the closely related Ariopsis felis, underscores a reproductive strategy focused on producing well-provisioned, developmentally advanced offspring capable of withstanding the challenges of the estuarine nursery environment, rather than broadcasting numerous small, vulnerable pelagic eggs.

As adults approach their maximum size, the physiological ceiling on somatic growth becomes apparent. The ultimate wet weight for Arius maculatus has been recorded at approximately 8750 grams [Wwi = approximately 8750 grams], derived from both commercial fishery landings and scientific sampling programs across its range. This asymptotic mass represents the point at which energetic intake is largely channeled into reproductive effort and maintenance rather than further increases in body length. Comparisons with other ariid species indicate that this maximum body mass is consistent with the upper size spectrum for the genus, reflecting a life history wherein individuals continue to grow slowly after maturity but at a decelerating rate. The attainment of this ultimate size is typically associated with older, dominant individuals that command the best foraging territories within the brackish water systems they inhabit.

Longevity records for the Spotted catfish, maintained under controlled conditions at a water temperature of 26.4 °C [T = 26.4 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years]. This relatively extended lifespan is consistent with the species’ delayed maturity, low fecundity, and large final body size, all hallmarks of a slow-paced life history strategy typical of many large ariids. In the wild, senescence and age-related mortality become apparent after this period, with older individuals showing reduced reproductive output and diminished physiological condition. The recorded longevity of a full decade (10 years) [am = 10 years] positions Arius maculatus among the longer-lived members of its family, a trait that likely confers resilience to sporadic recruitment failures by allowing multiple reproductive opportunities across an individual’s lifetime at a temperature of 26.4 °C [T = 26.4 °C].
